analysis.one_liner: Makes big-company executives criminally liable for negligently letting their corporations break the law.
analysis.headline: S. 1010 died in committee after being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, with no cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a crime for a top executive of a corporation earning more than $1 billion a year to negligently allow, or fail to prevent, their company from violating criminal or civil law. The bill covers crimes the company was convicted of, civil violations found or settled with a federal or state agency that harm the health, safety, finances, or personal data of at least 1% of the U.S. or a state's population, and repeat violations committed while the company was already operating under a court judgment, settlement, or deferred-prosecution agreement. A first offense carries up to one year in prison, a second offense up to three. The bill never moved past its referral to the Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who are harmed when large corporations break the law — consumers, workers, patients, and people whose financial or personal data is exposed — because senior executives, not just the company, would face personal criminal consequences for negligently allowing that harm.

how_it_helps.text: Executives of corporations with more than $1 billion in annual revenue would face criminal penalties, including prison, for negligently permitting or failing to prevent their company's violations of federal or state law.

The bill covers civil violations that affect the health, safety, finances, or personal data of at least 1% of the U.S. or a state's population, so large-scale harms to ordinary people would trigger executive liability, not just criminal convictions.

Repeat offenders get harsher treatment: a violation committed while the corporation was already operating under a judgment, settlement, or deferred-prosecution agreement counts, and a second offense carries up to three years in prison.

analysis.who_pays: Top executives of the roughly two hundred largest U.S. corporations and similar firms, who would face personal criminal fines and prison exposure for negligence, and the corporations' compliance and legal machinery, which would need to expand sharply.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes criminal liability for negligence, not intent: an executive who did not knowingly permit wrongdoing, and whose subordinates concealed it, could still face prosecution, which critics of strict-liability corporate crime laws argue is unfair and could push executive talent out of large firms.

The definition of executive officer turns on having 'responsibility and authority to take necessary measures to prevent or remedy violations,' which may be difficult to prove in large, complex organizations, and the liability triggers depend on the company already having been convicted, held liable, or settling — outcomes that itself often take years and can be negotiated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real deterrence: today large corporations routinely resolve misconduct through settlements and deferred-prosecution agreements paid out of company coffers, and senior executives rarely face personal consequences; this bill would put their freedom at stake when their negligence allows harms affecting millions. The cost is the risk of punishing executives for negligence rather than deliberate wrongdoing, and the possibility that liability would fall more on mid-level 'responsible' officers than on the CEO. The bill was never debated in committee, so none of these design questions were weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Corporate Executive Accountability Act on April 3, 2019.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No cosponsors ever joined, and the committee took no further action; there is no record of a hearing, a committee vote, or a Senate floor vote in the action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of the largest corporations, who finished the 116th Congress still facing no personal criminal liability for negligently allowing their companies to break the law, and the corporate legal and compliance industry that handles the settlements and deferred-prosecution agreements that remain the standard outcome instead.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic senator introduced the bill, no Republicans or other Democrats cosponsored it, and a Republican-led committee took no action, leaving the bill with support from only one side of the aisle.

industries.industry: Executives of large corporations ($1B+ annual revenue)
industries.note: Under current law, corporate wrongdoing is typically resolved with fines, settlements, or deferred-prosecution agreements paid by the company; individual executives rarely face criminal charges for negligence. The bill would expose them personally to fines and prison, which is why its core interest runs against the accountability ordinary people would gain.

Large firms' in-house legal and compliance departments and outside defense counsel currently manage misconduct through negotiated settlements and deferred-prosecution agreements. Executive-level criminal liability would expand their work but also strip away the arrangement that shields their clients personally.
